summary: How hostnames are resolved to IP addresses, and why the resolution process introduces security-relevant non-determinism — particularly the assumption that a hostname maps stably to the same IP address.

bounded_scope.covers: DNS hierarchical resolution, TTL expiration, caching behavior, and temporal instability between multiple resolution calls (TOCTOU).
bounded_scope.delegates: Network routing and IP reachability are delegated to concept.network-trust-boundaries; URI decomposition is delegated to concept.url-parsing.

learning_objectives: Explain how time-to-live (TTL) expiry permits non-deterministic resolution between validation and connection phases.
Derive why hostname allowlists fail to guarantee IP address safety without resolved IP pinning.
mental_model: DNS resolution translates a hostname into an IP address. This translation is not guaranteed to be stable: the same hostname can resolve to different IPs over time (TTL expiry, round-robin, geographic routing). When a system validates a hostname at one point in time and connects at another, the two resolutions may return different addresses. This gap is the foundation of DNS rebinding attacks.
mechanism: When an application resolves a hostname, it queries DNS recursively: local cache → system resolver → recursive resolver → authoritative nameserver. The response includes one or more IP addresses and a TTL (time-to-live) value. After TTL expiry, the next resolution may return a different IP. An attacker controlling a DNS zone can configure extremely short TTLs (e.g., 0 seconds) so that the first resolution returns an innocuous public IP (passing validation) and the second resolution returns a private IP (reaching the internal network). This is DNS rebinding.
security_relevance: SSRF — DNS rebinding bypasses hostname-based validation by changing resolution between check and connect
SSRF — Time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) between DNS validation and HTTP connection
Cache poisoning — DNS cache can be poisoned to redirect resolution
Subdomain takeover — dangling DNS records pointing to unclaimed resources
SSRF — Attacker-controlled hostnames with A records pointing directly to internal IPs (127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254) bypass hostname-based allowlists without needing DNS rebinding or TTL manipulation

common_assumptions.assumption: DNS resolution is stable — the same hostname always resolves to the same IP.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: TTL expiry, DNS rebinding attacks, round-robin DNS, and geographic routing all cause resolution to change between lookups.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF: A validate-then-connect pattern may validate against a public IP but connect to a private IP if DNS changes between the two lookups.

common_assumptions.assumption: Validating the hostname is equivalent to validating the destination IP.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: A hostname can resolve to any IP, including private/internal addresses. Hostname validation (e.g., checking against a domain allowlist) does not constrain the resolved IP.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF: An attacker-controlled hostname on an allowed domain can resolve to 127.0.0.1 or internal IPs.

common_assumptions.assumption: DNS resolution happens once per request.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: Some HTTP clients re-resolve DNS on redirect. A URL may initially resolve to a public IP, then after a redirect, the re-resolution may return a private IP.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF bypass via redirect chains that trigger re-resolution.

sources.title: OWASP - Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Documents DNS rebinding as a SSRF defense bypass technique and recommends resolving DNS once, validating the IP, then connecting to the resolved IP

sources.title: CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
sources.claim: Defines SSRF as a weakness where the web server receives a URL or similar request and retrieves contents without ensuring it is sent to the expected destination
